## Overview

In **4.2** we ran a GWAS on **one region** of one chromosome, inside our app. A whole-genome analysis is **22 or more** such jobs, each with large files. Run one after another in the app, that takes hours, and the app must stay open the whole time.

**Workflow tools** send each job to **its own cloud machine**, run them **at the same time**, save the results in your bucket, and shut the machines down. In this class we use **dsub**, the simplest of the three workflow tools in the Workbench, to run the 4.2 GWAS on **all 22 chromosomes in parallel**.

### Why this class matters

Most genomic analyses, and many others (imaging, long text, wearable data at minute level), are the **same step on many files**. Workflow tools make that fast, cheaper (each step gets the machine it needs, only while it runs), and **reproducible**. In *All of Us*, they also need a few settings that aren't in the general instructions: this class collects them in one place, tested.

### By the end you'll be able to

1. Say **when** to use a workflow tool instead of running code in your app
2. Describe the parts of a dsub job: **image**, **inputs**, **outputs**, **script**, and **logging**
3. Test a script **locally** first, then run it as **one** job, then as **many** (`--tasks`)
4. **Monitor** jobs with `dstat`, cancel them with `ddel`, and read their **logs** to fix errors
5. Compare **dsub**, **Cromwell** (WDL), and **Nextflow**, and know where to start with each

## Key concepts

### Two ways to run the same analysis

| | In your app (4.2) | With a workflow tool |
|---|---|---|
| **Where it runs** | on the app's machine | on **new cloud machines**, one per task |
| **How many at once** | one after another | **many at once** (in parallel) |
| **Machine size** | the app's size | **chosen per task**: big tasks get big machines |
| **While it runs** | the app must stay on; the notebook is busy | the app can do other things, or even be **stopped** |
| **Best for** | exploring, small data, plots | the **same steps on many files**: chromosomes, samples, batches |

👉 **Rule of thumb:** develop and test in your app; once a step works and has to run **many times** or on **big** files, move it to a workflow. Most class projects **don't need** workflows.

### Is a workflow cheaper?

Often **faster**; **cheaper** only sometimes: the total computing is about the same, but you pay for each machine only while it works, at the size it needs. In our tests, the 22 tasks added up to about 2 hours of machine time (on SSD disks) but ran at the same time, and the job cost well under $1: the workflow's gain is **time**. When it saves money and when it costs more: [Workflows for Beginners](workflows-for-beginners.qmd#is-it-cheaper).

### The words

| Word | Means |
|---|---|
| **Job** | one dsub command. It can have many **tasks**: here, one per chromosome |
| **Image** (container) | a packaged computer system with your software already installed (here, PLINK 2). Each task runs inside one |
| **Input** | a file the task needs. dsub **copies** it from a bucket onto the task's machine first (*localizing*) |
| **Output** | a file the task makes. dsub copies it **back** to your bucket at the end (*delocalizing*) |
| **Script** | the commands each task runs |
| **Logging** | where dsub saves each task's log. Your first stop when something fails |
| **Google Batch** | the Google Cloud service that creates, runs, and deletes the machines |

### How a dsub job runs

```{.default code-line-numbers="false"}
your app ── dsub ──► Google Batch ──► machine for chr1  ─┐
                                 ├──► machine for chr2  ─┤  each one: copy inputs in,
                                 ├──► ...                 ├─ run the script in the image,
                                 └──► machine for chr22 ─┘  copy outputs back, shut down
                                                           │
your bucket ◄──────────────── results and logs ───────────┘
```

### What *All of Us* needs: the settings

*All of Us* workspaces sit inside a **security perimeter**, and job machines have **no internet access**. So every job needs:

| Setting | Why |
|---|---|
| `--network global/networks/network` and `--subnetwork regions/us-central1/subnetworks/subnetwork` | the workspace's private network |
| `--use-private-address` | no public internet address |
| `--service-account` your account (`gcloud config get-value account`) | the job runs as you, so it can read *All of Us* data and write to your bucket |
| `--project` and `--user-project` `${GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT}` | your workspace's project pays, including for reading the *All of Us* files |
| `--image` from the ***All of Us* mirror** of Docker Hub | job machines can't reach Docker Hub itself, only Google's registries |
| `DSUB_CLOUD_SDK_IMAGE`, **pinned** | dsub's helper image (it copies the files). Its default is a moving tag; see below |
| `--disk-type pd-ssd` (recommended, not required) | dsub's default *standard* disk is slow to copy big files onto: see [What we learned](#what-we-learned) |

::: {.callout-warning title="Pin your versions: the November 2026 break"}
dsub uses a small helper image, Google's Cloud SDK, to copy files in and out. By default it uses whatever the latest version is. On **3 November 2026**, version 592 of that image came out, and every dsub job started to fail with ***exit status 127*** before running anything. The fix is to **pin** the version before it:

```{.bash code-line-numbers="false"}
export DSUB_CLOUD_SDK_IMAGE=gcr.io/google.com/cloudsdktool/google-cloud-cli:591.0.0-slim
```

The same goes for your own images: use a **version** tag (`plink2:alpha2.3_jan2020`), not `latest`, so the software can't change under you.
:::

In a **terminal**, the full set of settings looks like this. It's the command we used to test dsub in an *All of Us* workspace (November 2026, dsub 0.5.6), with one change: we've pinned the image's version.

```{.bash code-line-numbers="false"}
export DSUB_CLOUD_SDK_IMAGE=gcr.io/google.com/cloudsdktool/google-cloud-cli:591.0.0-slim
export ARTIFACT_REGISTRY_DOCKER_REPO=us-central1-docker.pkg.dev/all-of-us-rw-prod/aou-rw-gar-remote-repo-docker-prod
BUCKET=gs://your-bucket-name                                # from the Resources tab

dsub --provider google-batch \
  --project "${GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT}" --user-project "${GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT}" \
  --regions us-central1 \
  --network "global/networks/network" \
  --subnetwork "regions/us-central1/subnetworks/subnetwork" \
  --use-private-address \
  --service-account "$(gcloud config get-value account)" \
  --logging "${BUCKET}/dsub_test/logs" \
  --image "${ARTIFACT_REGISTRY_DOCKER_REPO}/ubuntu:24.04" \
  --output OUT="${BUCKET}/dsub_test/hello.txt" \
  --command 'echo "hello from dsub" > "${OUT}"' \
  --wait

gcloud storage cat "${BUCKET}/dsub_test/hello.txt"           # prints: hello from dsub
```

The notebook wraps these settings in an R function, `aou_dsub()`, so each job only lists what's **different**.

## Follow along in the Workbench

1. Open an *All of Us* **Jupyter** app, with this repository cloned (see the [GitHub guide](github-guide.qmd)).
2. Open `notebooks/workflows/workflows_dsub.ipynb`, with the **R** kernel. `gwas_one_chr.sh` must be in the same folder.
3. Run the cells in order. Parts 4 and 5 start cloud jobs: read on while they run.
4. Before you commit the notebook, **clear its outputs**: dsub's messages include your project ID and bucket address.

## Code walk-through

### One script, two places

The GWAS lives in a **shell script**, `gwas_one_chr.sh`. It reads every file name from an **environment variable**, so the **same script** runs in the app (Part 3) and in each job (Parts 4 and 5): only the variables change.

```{.bash code-line-numbers="false"}
set -euo pipefail
mkdir -p "${OUT_DIR}"

plink2 \
  --bfile "${BED%.bed}" \
  --keep "${KEEP}" \
  --maf 0.01 --geno 0.1 --hwe 1e-10 \
  --pheno "${PHENO}" --pheno-name t2d \
  --covar "${COVAR}" --covar-variance-standardize \
  --glm hide-covar firth-fallback \
  --out "${OUT_DIR}/chr${CHR}"
```

| Line | Does |
|---|---|
| `set -euo pipefail` | stop at the first error. Without it, a failed step could still look like a successful job |
| `--bfile "${BED%.bed}"` | the PLINK files, given as the `.bed` file's path; `${BED%.bed}` drops the `.bed` |
| `--keep` … `--glm` | our sample, the QC filters, and the association test from **4.2** |
| `--out "${OUT_DIR}/chr${CHR}"` | results named after the chromosome, e.g. `chr21.t2d.glm.logistic.hybrid` |

**Test it in the app first** (Part 3), on chromosome 21, reading the mounted files. A mistake shows up in a minute, for free.

### One job

```{.r code-line-numbers="false"}
job_chr21 <- aou_dsub(
  "--name", "gwas-chr21",
  "--image", PLINK_IMAGE,                                         # <1>
  "--machine-type", "n2-standard-2",
  "--disk-size", DISK_GB, "--disk-type", "pd-ssd",                # <2>
  "--script", "gwas_one_chr.sh",
  "--env", "CHR=21",
  "--input", paste0("BED=", CLINVAR_GS, "/clinvar.chr21.bed"),     # <3>
  "--input", paste0("BIM=", CLINVAR_GS, "/clinvar.chr21.bim"),
  "--input", paste0("FAM=", CLINVAR_GS, "/clinvar.chr21.fam"),
  "--input", paste0("KEEP=", KEEP_GS),
  "--input", paste0("PHENO=", PHENO_GS),
  "--input", paste0("COVAR=", COVAR_GS),
  "--output-recursive", paste0("OUT_DIR=", WORK_GS, "/test_chr21"),  # <4>
  wait = TRUE
)
```
1. PLINK 2 from the *All of Us* mirror, a pinned version.
2. Big enough for the inputs and outputs (set from the biggest ClinVar file), and **fast**: an SSD.
3. Every file the task needs must be an **input**, including the `.bim` and `.fam` files the script never names: the machine has nothing else.
4. A **folder** to copy back: everything the script writes in `OUT_DIR`.

The notebook then copies the job's results back and compares them with the app's: they should match.

### Many jobs: the tasks file

To run **many** tasks, give dsub a **tasks file**: a tab-separated table with **one row per task** and **one column per setting**. The heading says what each column is.

| `--env CHR` | `--input BED` | `--input BIM` | `--input FAM` | `--output-recursive OUT_DIR` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `gs://…/clinvar.chr1.bed` | `gs://…/clinvar.chr1.bim` | `gs://…/clinvar.chr1.fam` | `gs://…/gwas_clinvar/chr1` |
| 2 | `gs://…/clinvar.chr2.bed` | `gs://…/clinvar.chr2.bim` | `gs://…/clinvar.chr2.fam` | `gs://…/gwas_clinvar/chr2` |
| … | | | | |
| 22 | `gs://…/clinvar.chr22.bed` | … | … | `gs://…/gwas_clinvar/chr22` |

Settings that are the **same** for every task (the image, the script, the three small GWAS files) stay in the command, with `"--tasks", tasks_file` added. dsub starts all 22 tasks at once. The notebook doesn't wait: it checks on them with `dstat`.

```{.r code-line-numbers="false"}
dstat(job_all, "--summary")           # how many tasks are RUNNING, SUCCESS, FAILURE
dstat(job_all, "--wait", show = FALSE) # wait until every task has finished
```

dsub jobs **don't** appear on the Workbench's [Workflows tab](../workspace/workflows.qmd): that tab shows Cromwell and Nextflow workflows. Check dsub jobs with `dstat`.

### Combine

Each task wrote its results to its own folder. The notebook copies them to the app with `gcloud storage cp`, stacks them with `map(...) %>% bind_rows()`, and draws a **Manhattan plot**. These are **summary statistics** (one row per variant), so they're safe to look at. To **publish** them, follow the *All of Us* dissemination rules, as for any result.

## What we learned

We ran every step of this class in an *All of Us* workspace before teaching it (November 2026). Five lessons:

| What happened | Lesson |
|---|---|
| With dsub's **default disk** (a *standard* disk), chromosome 1 took **101 minutes**: 59 to copy its 27.7 GB `.bed` file onto the machine (about 8 MB a second), and 37 for PLINK. With an **SSD** disk (`--disk-type pd-ssd`), the same task took **8 minutes**: under 4 to copy (about 130 MB a second), about 2 for PLINK | **Most of a task's time can be copying files, not analysis.** Standard disks are cheap but slow, and slowest when small. For big inputs, use `--disk-type pd-ssd`: for a few minutes it costs about a cent more, and it saves machine time |
| On chromosome 21 (a small file), PLINK itself took about **2 seconds**; the whole task, a few minutes | starting a machine and copying files take minutes, whatever the job. That's why tiny jobs don't belong in a workflow |
| All 22 tasks on **standard** disks: about **580 minutes** (9½ hours) of machine time, added up; the whole job took **101 minutes**. On **SSD** disks: about **130 minutes** (2 hours) added up; 21 of the 22 tasks took **3 to 8 minutes** each | in parallel, a job takes as long as its **slowest** task. The SSD disks cut the machine time, and so the cost, by more than two thirds |
| On SSD disks, the whole job still took **32 minutes**, because one task (chromosome 4) **waited 30 minutes** for its machine. Its log started 30 minutes late; once it started, it took 2½ minutes | sometimes a task waits for a free machine, and you can't prevent it. `dstat`'s `start-time` doesn't show the wait (it equals `create-time`): the **first time stamp in the task's log** does |
| A long task's log repeated `You do not currently have an active account selected … Sleeping 10s` | harmless: dsub's log uploader, while the task runs. The job still succeeded and saved its log |

👉 **Find where the time goes:** each log line has a time stamp. The gap between `Localizing BED` and the next line is the copy; the gap after `PLINK v2` is the analysis.

## Try It Out

## ✋ Try It Out 1 · 5 minutes · while the 22 tasks run

Run only chromosomes **19 to 22**, in a new job. (Hint: the tasks file has a header row, so chromosome 1 is task 1.)

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Add the task numbers after the tasks file: `"--tasks", tasks_file, "19-22"`. Rows 19 to 22 are chromosomes 19 to 22, because the table is sorted by chromosome. This is also how you **rerun** only the tasks that failed.
:::

## ✋ Try It Out 2 · 5 minutes · Part 7

A classmate's job fails. The log says `plink2: Error: Failed to open …/clinvar.chr7.bim`. What's wrong? And how would you make the job cheaper?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The `.bim` file wasn't an **input**: the machine only has the files you give it with `--input`. PLINK needs the `.bed`, `.bim`, and `.fam` files together.

Cheaper: **spot** machines, `"--preemptible", "--retries", "2"`. They cost much less, but Google can stop them at any time; `--retries` starts a stopped task again. They suit short tasks like these.
:::

## When a job fails

**Read the log first.** dsub saves three per task in the `--logging` folder: `….log` (everything), `…-stdout.log` (what the script printed), and `…-stderr.log` (its errors).

| Symptom (in `dstat` or the log) | Likely cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `FAILURE` with **exit status 127**, before your script runs | dsub's helper image broke or can't be reached | pin `DSUB_CLOUD_SDK_IMAGE` to a version that works |
| An error about the **image**, or a job that never starts | the image isn't from a Google registry | put the *All of Us* mirror in front of Docker Hub images |
| `No such file or directory` | a file the script uses wasn't an **input** | add it with `--input` |
| `No space left on device` | the disk is too small | a bigger `--disk-size` |
| A task takes far longer than the others; in its log, a long gap after `Localizing BED` | copying a big file onto a slow **standard** disk (dsub's default) | `--disk-type pd-ssd` |
| `You do not currently have an active account selected` … `Sleeping 10s`, over and over | dsub's log uploader, while a long task runs | nothing: the task continues |
| One task finishes long after the others; its log **starts** late | it waited for a machine (none free, or the project's limit) | nothing: it runs once a machine is free |
| A task is killed, or PLINK runs out of memory | the machine is too small | a bigger `--machine-type` (e.g. `n2-highmem-4`) |
| `401 … Requester pays bucket access requires authentication`, then a retry | a short delay while the machine signs in | nothing: dsub retries, and the job continues |
| `Error: No variants remaining` | the filters removed every variant on that chromosome | check the filters, or leave that chromosome out |
| Tasks wait in the queue for a long time | the project's limit on machines or CPUs | wait, or run fewer tasks at a time |

**Cancel** a job (all its tasks): `ddel --provider google-batch --project "${GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT}" --location us-central1 --jobs JOB_ID`

## Scaling up: from ClinVar to ACAF

For a real GWAS, use the **ACAF** files (every variant common in at least one ancestry group). The steps are the same; the files are much **bigger**. In the *All of Us* tutorial, one ACAF chromosome (21) took about **60 minutes** to copy onto the machine and about **28 minutes** for PLINK, on a machine with 32 CPUs (`n2-highmem-32`) and a 400 GB disk. With files this big, an **SSD** disk matters even more (we haven't timed ACAF ourselves).

| | ClinVar (this class) | ACAF |
|---|---|---|
| **Variants** | those listed in ClinVar | all variants common in at least one ancestry group |
| **File sizes** (`.bed`) | 4 to 28 GB per chromosome, 293 GB in all (v9) | many times bigger |
| **Machine** | `n2-standard-2` | `n2-highmem-16` to `-32` |
| **Disk** | under 100 GB, SSD | 400 GB or more, SSD |
| **Time per task** | a few minutes | 1 to 2+ hours |
| **Cost** | under $1 in all | tens of dollars or more: **test on one chromosome first** |

Ways to save: **spot** machines (`--preemptible`, with `--retries`); **smaller tasks** (split each chromosome into regions with PLINK's `--from-bp` and `--to-bp`); and reading **only what you need**.

**Clean up** when you're done: job results stay in your bucket, and bucket storage is billed every month (`gcloud storage rm --recursive gs://…/data/workflows/test_chr21`).

## Cromwell and Nextflow

dsub is the **simplest** tool: one script, a table of tasks. It's great for **one step on many files**. When an analysis has **many steps** (e.g. QC → GWAS → plots), each using the outputs of the one before, a **workflow language** is easier: you describe the steps and how they connect, and the tool runs them in order, in parallel where it can, and can **resume** after a failure.

| | dsub | Cromwell | Nextflow |
|---|---|---|---|
| **You write** | a shell script and a dsub command | a **WDL** file (*Workflow Description Language*) and a JSON file of inputs | a **Nextflow** (`.nf`) file |
| **Best for** | one step on many files | multi-step pipelines; many published genomics workflows (e.g. GATK) | multi-step pipelines; the **nf-core** community pipelines |
| **Run from** | an app's terminal or notebook | the **[Workflows tab](../workspace/workflows.qmd)**, or `java -jar $CROMWELL_JAR run …` in an app | the **Workflows tab**, or `nextflow run …` in an app |
| **Ready-made workflows** | | [Dockstore](https://dockstore.org/) | [nf-core](https://nf-co.re/), [Dockstore](https://dockstore.org/) |
| **Learning curve** | low | medium | medium |

All three run their tasks on **Google Batch**, so the same *All of Us* rules apply: the private network, no public addresses, images from Google registries (or the *All of Us* mirror), and pinned versions. Each tool takes them in a short **configuration file**.

### Which one should I use?

All three gave the same answer in our tests, in about the same time. What differs is **how much you write**, **where you run it**, and **what's already written for you**.

| | What it does best | The catch (in *All of Us*) |
|---|---|---|
| **dsub** | The **simplest**: your shell script, plus a table with one row per file. The fastest way to run **one step on many files**. You can check each job with `dstat` and read its log | **One step per job**: for a pipeline, you run and check each step yourself. No **resume**. Jobs don't show on the Workflows tab. You need an app to start them |
| **Cromwell** (WDL) | The **Workflows tab**: no configuration file, no app, inputs in a **form**, a page to watch the job, and **batch jobs** from a table. **Call caching** skips steps that already finished. Many published genomics pipelines are written in WDL (GATK, the Broad Institute, [Dockstore](https://dockstore.org/)) | WDL is **wordy**: inputs, outputs, and runtime for every task. In an app (*run mode*) you need your own `cromwell.conf`, with the pinned helper image, and the app must stay on |
| **Nextflow** | **Short** pipeline files, and many tasks at once with very little code (`Channel.of(19..22)`). `-resume` restarts where a pipeline stopped. It **streams** bucket files instead of copying them, which helps when a tool reads only part of a file. The large [nf-core](https://nf-co.re/) community of pipelines | Every image must include `ps`. Google's job logs are blocked, so you read errors from the task's work folder. The Seqera web interface doesn't work. Ready-made nf-core pipelines download code and images from the internet: inside the perimeter, they need extra setup (we haven't tried one) |

👉 **A simple rule:**

1. **One step, many files** (one command per chromosome or sample): **dsub**.
2. **A published WDL pipeline**, or you'd rather **click than configure**: **Cromwell on the Workflows tab**.
3. **Your own multi-step pipeline**, or your lab already uses Nextflow: **Nextflow**.
4. **Not sure?** Start with dsub. It teaches every idea, and the script you write moves into a WDL `command` or a Nextflow `script` almost unchanged.

Your **collaborators** matter too: a pipeline in the language your lab or field already uses is easier to share and get help with.

### A task in each language

The same idea in each tool: PLINK on one chromosome, here allele frequencies of the common variants (`--maf 0.01 --freq`). They're based on the *All of Us* tutorial notebooks (folder *How to Use Workflow Tools* in the tutorial workspace), and **we ran both** in November 2026: both gave exactly the same frequencies as PLINK in the app (see [Tested: Cromwell and Nextflow](#tested-cromwell-and-nextflow)).

::: {.panel-tabset}
#### WDL (Cromwell)

```{.default code-line-numbers="false"}
version 1.0

workflow plink_freq {
  input {
    File bed
    File bim
    File fam
    String docker_image
  }
  call plink_check { input: bed = bed, bim = bim, fam = fam, docker_image = docker_image }
  output {
    File freq = plink_check.freq
  }
}

task plink_check {
  input {
    File bed
    File bim
    File fam
    String docker_image
  }
  command {
    plink2 --bed ~{bed} --bim ~{bim} --fam ~{fam} --maf 0.01 --freq --out chr
  }
  output {
    File freq = "chr.afreq"
  }
  runtime {
    docker: docker_image
    machineType: "n2-standard-2"
    disks: "local-disk 30 SSD"   # Cromwell copies the inputs here: SSD, as for dsub
  }
}
```

The inputs go in a JSON file (in an app) or a form (on the Workflows tab): the three `gs://` paths, and the image from the *All of Us* mirror.

#### Nextflow

```{.default code-line-numbers="false"}
params.plinkDir = "gs://vwb-aou-datasets-controlled/v9/wgs/short_read/snpindel/clinvar/plink_bed"
params.mirror   = "us-central1-docker.pkg.dev/all-of-us-rw-prod/aou-rw-gar-remote-repo-docker-prod"

process plink_check {
  container "${params.mirror}/biocontainer/plink2:alpha2.3_jan2020"
  cpus 2
  memory "8 GB"

  input:
  tuple val(chr), path(bed), path(bim), path(fam)

  output:
  path "chr${chr}.afreq"

  script:
  """
  plink2 --bed ${bed} --bim ${bim} --fam ${fam} --maf 0.01 --freq --out chr${chr}
  """
}

workflow {
  Channel.of(19..22)
    .map { c -> tuple(c, file("${params.plinkDir}/clinvar.chr${c}.bed"),
                         file("${params.plinkDir}/clinvar.chr${c}.bim"),
                         file("${params.plinkDir}/clinvar.chr${c}.fam")) }
    | plink_check
}
```

Nextflow runs one task per chromosome on its own, in parallel. Unlike dsub and Cromwell, it doesn't copy `gs://` inputs onto the machine first: it **mounts** the bucket and reads the files as it goes.
:::

### The *All of Us* settings for each

| Setting | Cromwell (`cromwell.conf`, backend `GCPBATCH`) | Nextflow (`nextflow.config`, executor `google-batch`) |
|---|---|---|
| Project | `project = "${GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT}"` | `google.project` |
| Where work files go | `root = "gs://your-bucket/workflows/cromwell-executions"` | `workDir = "gs://your-bucket/workflows/nextflow-scratch"` |
| Network | `virtual-private-cloud { network-name …, subnetwork-name … }` | `google.batch.network`, `google.batch.subnetwork` |
| No public address | `default-runtime-attributes { noAddress: true }` | `google.batch.usePrivateAddress = true` |
| Service account | `batch { compute-service-account = … }` | `google.batch.serviceAccountEmail` |
| Region | `batch { location = "us-central1" }` | `google.location = "us-central1"` |
| Paying for *All of Us* files | `filesystems { gcs { project = … } }` | `google.enableRequesterPaysBuckets = true` |
| Helper image (copies files), **pinned** | `google.cloud-sdk-image-url = "gcr.io/google.com/cloudsdktool/google-cloud-cli:591.0.0-slim"` | `google.batch.copyImage = "gcr.io/google.com/cloudsdktool/google-cloud-cli:591.0.0-alpine"` |
| Default image for tasks | | `process.container`: an image from the mirror that has `ps` (we used the PLINK image) |

The *All of Us* tutorial notebooks have complete configuration files; our [test notebook](https://github.com/CWML/All-of-Us-Training-Resources/blob/main/notebooks/workflows/workflows_cromwell_nextflow.ipynb) has the versions that worked, with the changes marked. Check three things in any configuration: that **every image** comes from a Google registry or the *All of Us* mirror (not straight from Docker Hub), that **helper images** use a pinned version, and that Nextflow's images include `ps`. The tutorials read the service account from `PET_SA_EMAIL`; it was empty in our app, so we used `gcloud config get-value account`, as for dsub.

### Three ways to run a workflow

| | Cromwell in an app (*run mode*) | Cromwell on the **Workflows tab** (*server mode*) | Nextflow in an app |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Start it with** | `java -jar $CROMWELL_JAR run plink_freq.wdl -i inputs.json` | the **Workflows** tab: add the workflow, then **+ New job** | `nextflow run plink_freq.nf -c nextflow.config` |
| **Inputs** | a JSON file | a **form**, built from the WDL (or an input table, for a batch) | in the `.nf` file, or `--param value` |
| **Settings** | your `cromwell.conf` | set by the Workbench: nothing to write | your `nextflow.config` |
| **Does the app need to stay on?** | **yes**, until it finishes | **no**: no app needed | **yes**, until it finishes |
| **Results** | `<work folder>/cromwell-executions/<workflow>/<id>/call-<task>/` | `<bucket>/<job name>/<workflow>/<id>/call-<task>/` | the work folder, or a `publishDir` you choose |

👉 **For most students, the Workflows tab is the easiest way to run WDL:** no configuration file, no app, and a page to watch the job on. How to use it: [the Workflows tab](../workspace/workflows.qmd).

### Tested: Cromwell and Nextflow

We ran each tool in an *All of Us* workspace in November 2026 (Jupyter app with OpenJDK 17, **Cromwell 92**, **Nextflow 25.10.2**; CDR v9), with the files from [our test notebook](https://github.com/CWML/All-of-Us-Training-Resources/blob/main/notebooks/workflows/workflows_cromwell_nextflow.ipynb). The check: allele frequencies on chromosome 21 (28,502 common variants), compared with PLINK in the app (0.5 minutes).

| Test | Result | Minutes | Same as the app? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cromwell *hello world*, in an app | ✅ worked (after the fix below) | 3.5 | |
| Cromwell PLINK, chromosome 21, in an app | ✅ worked | 4.3 | yes: all variants, difference 0 |
| Cromwell PLINK, chromosome 21, **Workflows tab** | ✅ worked | about 4 | yes: all variants, difference 0 |
| Cromwell *hello world* with an image straight from **Docker Hub** | ❌ failed | 3.5 | |
| Nextflow *hello*, in an app | ✅ worked (after the fix below) | 2.1 | |
| Nextflow PLINK, chromosomes 19 to 22 at once, in an app | ✅ worked | 3.4 | yes (chromosome 21: all variants) |

Each run took **3 to 4 minutes**, mostly starting machines: PLINK itself took 20 seconds to 2 minutes per chromosome. As for dsub, tiny jobs don't belong in a workflow.

#### What we learned testing Cromwell and Nextflow

| What happened | Lesson |
|---|---|
| Every Cromwell task in an app failed within 3 minutes: *"The job was stopped before the command finished"*. The task folder had only Cromwell's scripts (no `rc`, `stdout`, or `stderr`) | the **same break as dsub**: Cromwell copies files with Google's Cloud SDK image, and version 592 broke it. **Pin version 591** in `cromwell.conf` (`google.cloud-sdk-image-url`). The *All of Us* tutorial's configuration doesn't have this line |
| The **Workflows tab** ran the same WDL with no fix | the tab runs its own Cromwell, set up by the Workbench, so it wasn't affected |
| The Nextflow *hello* task failed: *"Command 'ps' required by nextflow to collect task metrics cannot be found"* | Nextflow runs `ps` **inside your container** to measure each task. The tutorial's default image (`ubuntu-slim`) doesn't have it, and nor does the official `ubuntu` image. Use an image that does (our PLINK image did), or install the `procps` package in your own |
| Nextflow said *"Permission denied for all log views"* | *All of Us* blocks Google's job logs. Read the failed task's own files instead: `.command.err` and `.command.log`, in its work folder (`…/nextflow-scratch/xx/…`) |
| Cromwell printed `MANIFEST_UNKNOWN … falling back to OCI manifest` | harmless: Cromwell couldn't fingerprint the image (used only to reuse earlier results) |
| The image straight from Docker Hub failed | as for dsub: use the ***All of Us* mirror** for every image, in every tool |
| The Workflows tab's bucket list opened on `dataproc-staging-…`, with *"0 workflows found"* | choose **your workspace bucket** in the list; the tab then finds `.wdl` files in all its folders |
| Halfway through, the notebook's R session restarted, and every result in memory was gone | files on disk and in the bucket survive. Rerun the **setup** cells, not *Run All* (it would rerun every test). In run mode, a workflow also stops if the **app** stops: watch the auto-stop setting |

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Instructor tip"}
Tested November 2026 (*All of Us* Jupyter app, CDR v9): dsub 0.5.6 (the chromosome 21 job, all 22 tasks, chromosome 1 on standard and SSD disks), Cromwell 92 in run mode and on the Workflows tab, and Nextflow 25.10.2 in an app. Not tested: Nextflow from the Workflows tab, batch jobs (input tables) on the Workflows tab, and the ACAF files. The pinned 591 helper images will be deleted by Google about 12 months after release: **check around November 2027** and move to a newer version that works. The tutorials note that the Nextflow web interface (Seqera) doesn't work in *All of Us* workspaces, because they have no internet access, and that Nextflow 26.04 has a stricter syntax than the app's 25.10. Job machines and bucket storage are billed to the workspace's pod and don't appear in the app cost estimate. For a 2-hour class, demo the Workflows tab live (about 10 minutes, including the 4-minute run) rather than run mode.
:::

## Instructor notes

## Instructor tip: timing and pitfalls

- **Start the 22-task job before the break**, or before Part 8: it runs while you teach. Machines take a few minutes to start.
- Students in the same workspace share the project's **limits** on machines and CPUs. In a large class, have pairs share one run.
- The commonest failures are **settings**, not code: a missing network flag, an image straight from Docker Hub, or a helper image that changed. The settings in `aou_dsub()` were tested in November 2026; if jobs fail with exit status 127 before the script runs, check the [dsub issues on GitHub](https://github.com/DataBiosphere/dsub/issues) for a newer working helper version.
- The **comparison** in Part 4 (app vs job) is the key check. A small difference in p-values comes from the PLINK version (the image's 2020 version vs the app's newer one): a good moment to talk about **pinning and reporting versions**.
- dsub's printed messages include the workspace project ID, the bucket address, and your service account: **clear outputs** before committing, and share the notebook through GitHub, never by downloading it.
- Students may look for their jobs on the **Workflows** tab: dsub jobs aren't there (it shows Cromwell and Nextflow). Use `dstat`.

## Key takeaways

- Use a **workflow tool** when the **same step** has to run on **many** or **big** files: each task gets its own machine, and they run **in parallel**
- A dsub job is an **image**, a **script**, **inputs** (copied onto the machine), **outputs** (copied back), and a **log**
- **Test small first:** the script in the app, then one job, then all of them
- **Every file a task needs must be an input**: the machine has nothing else
- In *All of Us*: the private network, no public address, images from the **mirror**, and **pinned** versions
- `dstat` to monitor, `ddel` to cancel, and the **log** to find out why a task failed, or where its time went
- **Copying** big files can take longer than the analysis: use an **SSD** disk (`--disk-type pd-ssd`)
- For **multi-step** pipelines, use a workflow language: **WDL** with Cromwell, or **Nextflow**. The **Workflows tab** runs WDL with no configuration file and no app
- **Pin helper images** in every tool (dsub, Cromwell, Nextflow): one new version broke both dsub and Cromwell in November 2026

## Further reading

- [dsub on GitHub](https://github.com/DataBiosphere/dsub): documentation, including [input and output files](https://github.com/DataBiosphere/dsub/blob/main/docs/input_output.md) and [job control](https://github.com/DataBiosphere/dsub/blob/main/docs/job_control.md)
- [Verily Workbench: workflows](https://support.workbench.verily.com/docs/): Cromwell, Nextflow, and dsub in the Workbench
- [OpenWDL](https://openwdl.org/) (the WDL language) and [Nextflow documentation](https://www.nextflow.io/docs/latest/)
- [Dockstore](https://dockstore.org/) and [nf-core](https://nf-co.re/): ready-made, published workflows
- The *All of Us* tutorial workspace: *How to Use Workflow Tools* (dsub, Cromwell, Nextflow notebooks)
